# Negative

Orthogonally adjacent pairs outside the exception list fail every listed relationship. The scope, direction and exceptions state exactly which pairs are covered.

Neighbouring means orthogonally adjacent. Without this declaration, missing dots or X/V clues imply nothing. For all white dots given, forbid `{"op":"difference","value":1}`; for black dots, forbid `{"op":"ratio","value":2}`; for X clues, forbid `{"op":"sum","value":10}`; for V clues, forbid `{"op":"sum","value":5}`. List the marked pairs in `except`. An empty exceptions list exempts no pairs.

For relation-specific marking, use separate negative declarations and separate exception lists. A 1–2 pair satisfies both white and black relationships; exempting only black-marked pairs from a white negative does not exempt that pair. To apply both negatives only to completely unmarked pairs, put both relationships in one declaration and exempt every dotted pair. With no exceptions and no scope or direction limit, a difference-1 negative is the global non-consecutive rule. Negative reads printed digits; positive Pair and Kropki read effective values after modifiers.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| relations | The relationships to forbid, each with its operation and any required value. | Required. |
| except | The cell pairs exempt from the negative rule. | Required. |
| within | Groups limiting the pairs covered by the rule. | Absent; no inferred value. |
| direction | The chosen diagonal or neighbour orientation, as named in the definition. | Absent; no inferred value. |

## Maths

Class: **first-order**.

The [shared predicates](https://rules.sudoku-sleuth.com/predicates.md) define the notation and every named predicate.

```text
∀a,b∈C: ∀r∈relations:
  cellIndex(a)<cellIndex(b) ∧ orth(a,b)
  ∧ (if present(within) then ∃G∈unwrap(within): a∈G ∧ b∈G else true)
  ∧ (if present(direction) then (unwrap(direction)="horizontal" ∧ row(a)=row(b)) ∨ (unwrap(direction)="vertical" ∧ col(a)=col(b)) else true)
  ∧ ¬(∃p∈except: |p|=2 ∧ {a,b}={p[0],p[1]})
  → ¬pairRelation(r,D(a),D(b))
```

Every orthogonally neighbouring pair in scope and outside except fails every listed relationHolds check over D digits. within limits pairs to a common listed group; direction limits their orientation. Either dot colour exempts the pair from both Kropki negatives when both share except.

The shift relation is defined for integer values.

# Lookup

A number gives a position in an ordered cell list. The number at that position obeys the stated relation with a fixed target, another cell, or the index cell itself.

Positions start at one. Add `offset` before looking up the position. The result must be a whole number within the list. `indexChannel` supplies the position; `channel` supplies the compared numbers. Both read printed digits by default.

[Index](index.md), [Index Line](index-line.md), [Numbered Room](numbered-room.md) and [Pointing Arrow](pointing-arrow.md) use the same bounded lookup with their own strips and targets.

| offset | Offset added to the index. | 0. |
| target | Fixed comparison target. | Absent; use targetCell or the index cell. |
| targetCell | Cell supplying the target. | Absent; use the index cell. |
| relation | Shared relation from lookup result to target. | difference 0 (equal). |

# Aggregate Equation

Compare two arithmetic expressions built from aggregate operands. Each term multiplies an operand raised to a nonnegative integer power by its coefficient. Each side sums or multiplies its terms. # Route

Construct one named route with distinct cells and allowed steps. A loop closes its last cell to its first and has at least three cells. An open route may specify endpoints. Covering visits every cell in scope once. Required and forbidden edges are undirected. Touch restrictions exclude consecutive steps; proper interior step crossings are checked separately. Crossings mean interior intersections of straight segments of any length, including bishop and knight steps; shared endpoints and collinear overlaps are excluded. The same name in another declaration refers to this same route, including its order.

A long step passing through a visited cell is allowed by `crossings false` when that cell is an endpoint of the other step. Only intersections strictly inside both steps count; collinear overlaps do not count.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| name | The shared route name. | Required. |
| scope | Cells the route may use. | Required. |
| move | Allowed step geometry. | orthogonal. |
| loop | Require a simple closed cycle. | false. |
| cover | Visit every cell in scope. | false. |
| minimum | Minimum number of visited cells. | 1. |
| maximum | Maximum number of visited cells. | Absent; use scope size. |
| startCell | Required first cell of an open route. | Absent; either endpoint. |
| endCell | Required last cell of an open route. | Absent; either endpoint. |
| through | Cells that must be visited. | Empty set. |
| requiredEdges | Undirected edges the route must use. | Empty list. |
| forbiddenEdges | Undirected edges the route must avoid. | Empty list. |
| noTouch | Forbid this move between nonconsecutive route cells. | Absent; no additional touch condition. |
| crossings | Allow crossings between straight steps of any length. | false. |

## Maths

Class: **existential**.

The [shared predicates](predicates.md) define the notation and operations.

```text
let L=routeAnswer(name); simpleRoute(L,scope,move,routeClosed(name)) ∧ minimum>=1 ∧ minimum<=|L| ∧ |L|<=(if present(maximum) then unwrap(maximum) else |scope|) ∧ (cover → routeCells(L)=scope) ∧ through⊆routeCells(L) ∧ (present(startCell) → ¬loop ∧ |L|>0 ∧ L[0]=unwrap(startCell)) ∧ (present(endCell) → ¬loop ∧ |L|>0 ∧ L[|L|-1]=unwrap(endCell)) ∧ (∀e∈requiredEdges: |e|=2 ∧ routeEdge(L,e[0],e[1],loop)) ∧ (∀e∈forbiddenEdges: |e|=2 ∧ ¬routeEdge(L,e[0],e[1],loop)) ∧ (present(noTouch) → noRouteTouch(L,unwrap(noTouch),loop)) ∧ (crossings ∨ ¬routeCrosses(L,L,loop,loop))
```

# Extremum

Each marked digit is smaller than all its unmarked neighbours for a minimum, or larger for a maximum. Exhaustive marking also constrains every unmarked cell.

Neighbours here are orthogonally adjacent cells outside the entire marked set. With `type "max" exhaustive false`, this gives fortress cells: adjacent marked cells are not compared. To compare a minimum or maximum with every orthogonally adjacent cell, declare that cell on its own. With `exhaustive true`, each unmarked cell must have a strictly smaller neighbour for min, or a strictly larger neighbour for max.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| type | The mode named in the definition, such as min or max. | Required. |
| cells | The marked cells, for example r1c1-r1c2-r2c2. | Required. |
| exhaustive | Whether every occurrence is marked, so unmarked cells obey the opposite condition. | Required. |
| neighbourhood | The move defining neighbours. | orthogonal. |
| boundary | Compare marked cells only with neighbours outside the marked set. | true. |
| channel | Read printed digits (D) or effective values (V). | D. |

## Maths

Class: **first-order**.

The [shared predicates](https://rules.sudoku-sleuth.com/predicates.md) define the notation and every named predicate.

```text
(∀a∈cells: extremumAt(a,{b∈C:moveRelation(neighbourhood,a,b) ∧ (¬boundary ∨ b∉cells)},type,channel))
∧ (exhaustive → ∀a∈C: a∉cells → ∃b∈C: moveRelation(neighbourhood,a,b) ∧ extremumAt(b,{a},type,channel))
```

Marked extrema compare the selected neighbours, excluding the marked set when boundary is true. Exhaustive marking retains the requirement for a strictly lower or higher neighbour at each unmarked cell.

# Decoration

The specified drawn marks are decorative only. They carry no rule, and tools must derive no constraints from them. Other marks on the same cells retain their own rules.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cells | The cells covered by the marks; list every cell of a region. | Required. |
| note | A description of which marks to ignore. | Omitted. |

Use the common `element "..."` metadata to identify a particular drawn element. Use the same element ID on declarations referring to the same mark; different marks need different IDs. A decoration and a constraining declaration with the same element ID and overlapping cells produce a warning. A note describes the marks; tools must not interpret it as a rule.

## Maths

Class: **first-order**.

The [shared predicates](https://rules.sudoku-sleuth.com/predicates.md) define the common notation.

```text
true
```

Decoration adds no condition. Semantic comparison drops it from the logical meaning and retains its cells, note, element ID and source as metadata. Negation and conditions are not accepted on decoration; file-level negation leaves decorations unchanged.

## Example

```rules
sudoku 9x9
decoration r1c1-r1c2-r2c2 note "The grey ribbon is decorative." element "grey-ribbon"
```

Satisfies the declaration: r1c1=1, r1c2=2, r2c2=3. The ribbon imposes no relationship between these digits.

There is no breaking assignment: `true` accepts every assignment. For example, r1c1=9, r1c2=1, r2c2=7 also satisfies the declaration. The other puzzle rules still apply.
